claims.text: The proposed rapidly solidified Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The as-cast alloy contains metastable Mg-rich solid solutions.
The as-cast alloy initially contains only limited amounts of stable intermetallic phases.
Thermal exposure from approximately 200 to 700 °C will induce decomposition of the metastable Mg-rich solid solutions.
Decomposition of the metastable solid solutions produces stable intermetallic compounds.
The phase transformation causes local elemental redistribution and changes interface morphology.
Magnesium becomes enriched in newly formed intermetallic phases.
Formation of Mg-enriched intermetallic phases depletes protective elements such as Al from the matrix.
Solute partitioning during decomposition changes the alloy's passivation or pitting behavior.
Solute partitioning and intermetallic formation change the composition of the high-temperature oxide scale.
Microstructural decomposition alters pathways for high-temperature oxide-scale formation.
Heat-treated specimens will have corrosion potentials or current densities measurably different from those of as-cast controls.
Heat-treated specimens will have high-temperature oxidation mass gains measurably different from those of as-cast controls.
If temperature or duration is insufficient to decompose the metastable phases, corrosion and oxidation behavior will not differ significantly from the as-cast baseline.
Extremely high temperatures or prolonged aging may cause complete phase transformation and behavior dominated by stable intermetallics.
The direction and rate of the environmental-property changes depend on Mg content and the other alloying elements.
As-cast and heat-treated specimens of identical composition and preparation history can serve as the controlled comparison.
